Iliac obstruction typically presents with unilateral symptoms and unilateral absence of femoral and distal pulses.
Distal obstruction involves claudication in the calf and foot with palpable femoral and popliteal pulses.
Femoropopliteal obstruction usually presents with unilateral calf claudication and palpable femoral pulses.
Aortoiliac obstruction (Leriche syndrome) is characterized by buttock/thigh/calf claudication, bilateral pulse absence, and impotence.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1021: "Aortoiliac obstruction Claudication in the buttocks, thighs and calves Femoral and distal pulses absent in both limbs Bruit over the aortoiliac region Impotence (Leriche)"

statement: A 58-year-old patient presents with symptoms suggestive of an iliac stenosis. On initial examination at rest, the distal pulses are found to be palpable despite the presence of significant claudication. The clinician requests the patient to walk until claudication develops and then re-examines the pulses. What is the expected physiological finding regarding the pulses in this specific scenario, and why does it occur?
options: Pulses disappear because of a paradoxical continuous-wave Doppler shift
Pulses remain the same as iliac stenosis rarely affects distal pulse pressure
Pulses remain palpable due to the highly developed collateral circulation
Pulses become more prominent as the machinery murmur increases flow
Pulses disappear because vasodilation below the obstruction reduces pulse pressure
correctOption: Pulses disappear because vasodilation below the obstruction reduces pulse pressure
optionExplanations: Doppler shift is a measurement mechanism, not the physiological cause of pulse disappearance.
Iliac stenosis significantly impacts distal pulse pressure during exercise-induced vasodilation.
Highly developed collaterals allow rest pulses to be palpable, but exercise changes this state.
Machinery murmurs indicate AV fistulas and are not related to the typical presentation of iliac stenosis.
Vasodilation occurring below the obstruction during exercise reduces the pulse pressure, causing the pulse to disappear.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1021: "In this case, exercise (walking until claudication develops) usually causes the pulse to disappear as vasodilation occurs below the obstruction, thereby reducing the pulse pres - sure."

statement: A clinician is using a hand-held Doppler ultrasound probe to evaluate a patient with suspected peripheral arterial disease. During the assessment, the signal obtained over the dorsalis pedis artery is identified as monophasic. How should the clinician evaluate this finding compared to a normal arterial signal, and what does it indicate about the state of the vessel?
options: The signal indicates the extent of disease, as a normal artery should be triphasic
The signal confirms a machinery murmur indicative of an arteriovenous fistula
A monophasic signal is normal in elderly patients
Monophasic signals only occur when assessing small vessels with a sphygmomanometer
A normal artery has a monophasic signal, whereas diseased ones are triphasic
correctOption: The signal indicates the extent of disease, as a normal artery should be triphasic
optionExplanations: Normal arteries produce triphasic signals; biphasic or monophasic signals signify the presence and extent of disease.
A machinery murmur is an auscultatory finding, whereas monophasic signals describe a Doppler waveform pattern.
Monophasic signals are not normal; they indicate disease regardless of age.
Doppler signals provide waveform data regardless of whether a sphygmomanometer is used simultaneously.
The relationship is inverted; triphasic is normal and monophasic indicates disease.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1022: "a normal artery has a triphasic signal whereas a diseased artery may have a biphasic or monophasic signal depending on the extent of disease."

statement: A patient with severe lower limb ischaemia and an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) that is low is being considered for angiography to identify the anatomical location of the disease. Which of the following evaluations must the clinician prioritize before proceeding with intravenous contrast agents in this patient?
options: The likelihood of contrast agents inducing an aortic aneurysm
The potential for contrast to cause polycythaemia
The potential for contrast to improve high blood viscosity
The risk of the contrast agent exacerbating renal impairment
The risk of contrast agents causing intermittent claudication
correctOption: The risk of the contrast agent exacerbating renal impairment
optionExplanations: Aortic aneurysms coexist with disease but are not induced by contrast agents.
Polycythaemia is typically caused by smoking or associated with cancer, not contrast agents.
Contrast agents do not treat high blood viscosity; viscosity is related to smoking or cancer.
Contrast agents used during angiography can exacerbate pre-existing renal impairment (low eGFR).
Intermittent claudication is a symptom of arterial disease, not a side effect of contrast.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1021: "renal impairment (raised serum creatinine and low estimated glomerular fltration rate) may be caused by drugs and may be exacerbated by intravenous contrast agents used during angiography."

statement: During a physical examination of a patient with suspected gangrene of the foot, the clinician performs a capillary refill test by compressing the nail bed and then releasing it to observe the return of color. Which finding is most consistent with the clinical judgment of severe ischaemia in this specific limb?
options: Immediate color return with dependent rubor
optionExplanations: 1 second is faster than the normal range and does not indicate ischaemia.
2–3 seconds is the normal time for capillary refill.
Immediate return is not characteristic of the capillary refill delay found in severe ischemia.
In severe ischaemia, the capillary refill time may be prolonged up to 10 seconds.
While 5 seconds is abnormal, the text specifically identifies 10 seconds as the marker for severe ischaemia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1021: "normally this takes 2–3 seconds but may be prolonged to 10 seconds in severe ischaemia."

statement: An elderly patient presents for a routine vascular check-up. While examining the popliteal pulses, the clinician finds them exceptionally easy to appreciate. Which additional clinical finding would lead to the synthesized suspicion that the patient has a popliteal artery aneurysm rather than just a prominent pulse?
options: Presence of a triphasic Doppler signal
Loss of the natural concavity of the popliteal fossa
A machinery murmur in the popliteal fossa
Return of color within 2 seconds of elevation
correctOption: Loss of the natural concavity of the popliteal fossa
optionExplanations: A triphasic signal is a normal Doppler finding and does not specifically suggest an aneurysm.
Suspected popliteal aneurysm is characterized by a prominent pulse combined with the loss of the fossa's natural concavity.
Machinery murmurs indicate arteriovenous fistulas, not aneurysms.
Normal capillary refill/color return does not assist in diagnosing an aneurysm of the popliteal artery.
Buttock claudication is associated with proximal aortoiliac or iliac disease, not popliteal aneurysms.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1021: "a popliteal artery aneurysm should be suspected if the popliteal pulse is prominent with concomitant loss of the natural concavity of the popliteal fossa."

coreConcept: Clinical decision for intervention in PAD
statement: A 70-year-old patient presents with mild symptomatology of lower limb ischaemia. The patient is otherwise stable and ambulatory. What is the standard management principle regarding the use of invasive special investigations like angiography or surgical reconstruction in this specific case?
options: Special investigations must be performed to exclude asymptomatic coronary disease
Invasive treatment and special investigations are often not required for mild symptoms
Investigations should only be performed if the patient has a machinery murmur
Surgical reconstruction is mandatory if pedal pulses are clinically palpable
All patients require angioplasty immediately to prevent gangrene
correctOption: Invasive treatment and special investigations are often not required for mild symptoms
optionExplanations: While coronary disease may coexist, PAD management decisions focus on the limb symptoms first.
The decision to intervene can often be made without special investigations if the symptoms are mild.
Machinery murmurs indicate AV fistulas, which is a separate clinical finding from general PAD assessment.
If pulses are palpable and symptoms are mild, surgical intervention is generally not indicated.
Angioplasty is not indicated for all patients, especially those with mild symptoms.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1021: "Most patients with symptomatic lower limb ischaemia pres - ent with mild symptomatology and do not require invasive treatment, such as angioplasty or surgical reconstruction, and the decision of whether or not to intervene can often be made without recourse to special investigations."

statement: A clinician auscultates over the femoral artery of a patient with suspected chronic arterial disease. No bruit is heard. Which of the following statements best explains why the absence of an arterial bruit is an unreliable clinical sign for excluding significant vascular disease?
options: Tight stenoses often do not have bruits
Only monophasic Doppler signals produce audible bruits
A bruit is only present if there is a machinery murmur
Bruits disappear once a patient reaches the age of 50
Bruits are only heard in veins, not arteries
correctOption: Tight stenoses often do not have bruits
optionExplanations: An arterial bruit is an unreliable sign because tight stenoses often lack them.
Bruits are heard via stethoscope, whereas monophasic signals are Doppler findings; they are independent.
A machinery murmur indicates a fistula, whereas a simple bruit indicates a stenosis.
Bruits are related to the physical state of the vessel (stenosis), not the age of the patient.
Bruits are specifically arterial signs indicating turbulent flow.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1021: "However, it is an unreliable clinical sign as tight stenoses often do not have bruits."

statement: While auscultating the femoral artery of a patient who recently underwent a vascular procedure, a continuous machinery murmur is detected. How should this finding be distinguished from a standard arterial bruit?
options: It suggests the presence of a popliteal aneurysm
It indicates a very tight stenosis
It is a normal finding after exercise
It confirms the presence of monophasic flow
optionExplanations: Popliteal aneurysms present with prominent pulses, not machinery murmurs.
A continuous machinery murmur is the characteristic clinical sign of an arteriovenous fistula.
A standard bruit indicates stenosis, but a continuous machinery murmur is specific for a fistula.
Machinery murmurs are never normal findings.
Monophasic flow is a Doppler waveform pattern, not an auscultatory murmur.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1021: "A continuous ‘machinery’ murmur over an artery usually indicates an arteriovenous fstula."

coreConcept: Assessing systolic pressure in small vessels
statement: A patient presents with advanced peripheral arterial disease where pedal pulses are clinically impalpable. The clinician needs to assess the systolic pressure in the small vessels of the foot. How can Doppler ultrasound equipment be applied to achieve this in a patient where pulses cannot be palpated?
options: It can be used in conjunction with a sphygmomanometer
It can only be used if a machinery murmur is present
It must be used only when the signal is triphasic
It is only applicable if the patient has intermittent claudication
It is used to calculate the blood viscosity rather than pressure
correctOption: It can be used in conjunction with a sphygmomanometer
optionExplanations: Doppler ultrasound can be used with a sphygmomanometer to assess systolic pressure even when pulses are impalpable.
Machinery murmurs indicate fistulas and are not required to measure systolic pressure.
Signal quality (monophasic/triphasic) does not prevent the measurement of pressure.
Pressure assessment is useful for many PAD stages, not just intermittent claudication.
Doppler assesses flow velocity and pressure, not the chemical viscosity of blood.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1021: "Doppler ultrasound equipment can be used in conjunction with a sphygmomanometer to assess systolic pressure in small vessels. This is possible even when the arterial pulse cannot be palpated."

statement: A 72-year-old patient is diagnosed with peripheral arterial disease (PAD) in the lower legs. Why is it standard practice to perform an ECG and potentially a cerebral arterial assessment in this patient, even if they have no cardiac or neurological symptoms?
options: Atherosclerosis is often a multisystem disease affecting coronary and cerebral trees
A normal ECG is required before a capillary refill test can be performed
ECGs are required to calculate the ankle–brachial pressure index
Cerebral trees must be assessed to identify the site of intermittent claudication
Doppler probes can only function if the cardiac rhythm is normal
correctOption: Atherosclerosis is often a multisystem disease affecting coronary and cerebral trees
optionExplanations: The presence of leg arterial disease suggests disease in other arterial trees, such as coronary (50%) and cerebral (25-50%).
Capillary refill is a physical exam maneuver independent of ECG results.
ECGs are for cardiac health, not for calculating pressure indices.
Claudication occurs in the limbs, not the cerebral tree.
Doppler probes function regardless of rhythm, though rhythm affects signal interpretation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1021: "athero - sclerosis is often a multisystem disease process; the presence of arterial disease in the leg is suggestive of disease in other arterial trees, including the coronary (50%) and cerebral (25–50%) trees."

statement: When examining a patient for lower limb occlusive disease, it is standard surgical practice to examine several specific arteries. Along with the pedal pulses, which of the following combinations of areas should be examined simultaneously to check for coexisting vascular issues?
options: Only the dorsalis pedis and popliteal arteries
The femoral artery and the jugular venous pressure
The axillary and subclavian arteries only
Femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, and the abdomen
correctOption: Femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, and the abdomen
optionExplanations: This is an incomplete list; the femoral artery and abdomen are also vital components.
Jugular venous pressure is a venous assessment, not part of the standard arterial pulse examination for PAD.
Axillary and subclavian arteries are not the primary focus of lower limb occlusive disease exams.
While carotids are relevant for multisystem disease, the standard limb exam focus is different.
Standard practice includes the femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis arteries, plus the abdomen for aortic aneurysm.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1021: "It is standard practice to examine the femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis arteries together with the abdomen for an aortic aneurysm, which may coexist with lower limb occlusive disease."

statement: A patient presents with unilateral claudication in the thigh and calf. Upon physical examination, you detect a bruit over the iliac region. Which specific pulse finding would most strongly support a diagnosis of unilateral iliac obstruction in this patient?
options: Unilateral absence of femoral and distal pulses
Palpable femoral and popliteal pulses with absent ankle pulses
Palpable femoral pulse with absent popliteal pulse
Prominent popliteal pulse with loss of fossa concavity
correctOption: Unilateral absence of femoral and distal pulses
optionExplanations: Bilateral absence of femoral pulses is characteristic of aortoiliac obstruction.
Unilateral iliac obstruction is marked by unilateral claudication and the unilateral absence of femoral and distal pulses.
This finding describes distal obstruction.
Palpable femoral with absent distal is characteristic of femoropopliteal obstruction.
This finding describes a popliteal aneurysm.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1021: "Iliac obstruction Unilateral claudication in the thigh and calf and sometimes the buttock Bruit over the iliac region Unilateral absence of femoral and distal pulses"

coreConcept: Surgical Morbidity of Pelvic Vein Interventions
statement: A 35-year-old woman with symptomatic pudendal varicosities and left ovarian vein incompetence is evaluating her surgical options. She is concerned about postoperative recovery and the risk of complications from invasive procedures. Which management strategy has largely replaced historical open surgical resections to reduce peri-procedural and post-procedural morbidity while ensuring high success rates?
options: Transabdominal ligation of internal iliac veins
Sclerotherapy of the pudendal venous plexus
optionExplanations: Ligation of the internal iliac veins is not the standard superseding intervention for ovarian vein incompetence.
Extraperitoneal resection is a historical procedure that has been largely replaced by percutaneous methods.
Sclerotherapy is not described as the primary replacement for open surgical resection of ovarian veins.
Open excision is associated with higher morbidity compared to modern percutaneous embolisation techniques.
Percutaneous embolisation has superseded open surgery by providing lower morbidity and high success.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1042: "Historical open surgical procedures (extraperitoneal resection of ovarian veins) have now largely been superseded by percutaneous pelvic vein embolisation ( Figure 62.29 ), reducing peri- and post- procedural morbidity while maintaining high success rates."

coreConcept: Clinical Features of Superficial Vein Thrombosis
statement: A patient presents with a painful, red, palpable cord-like structure along the course of a tortuous vein in the calf. What is the clinical term used for this formation of a semisolid coagulum within the superficial venous system?
optionExplanations: Post-thrombotic syndrome is a late complication following a deep vein thrombosis.
Lipodermatosclerosis refers to skin changes associated with chronic venous insufficiency and PTS.
Deep vein thrombosis involves the deep system rather than the superficial system mentioned.
Thrombophlebitis is the specific term used for thrombosis within the superficial venous system.
Phlegmasia cerulea dolens is a severe form of deep vein thrombosis with limb-threatening ischemia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1042: "Venous thrombosis is the formation of a semisolid coagulum within the venous system and may occur in the superfcial system (super - fcial vein thrombosis [SVT] or “thrombophlebitis”) or the deep system (deep vein thrombosis [DVT])."

statement: Which clinical complication of the leg is a known subsequent risk for patients who have previously suffered from a deep vein thrombosis of the lower limb?
optionExplanations: Raynaud phenomenon is a vasospastic disorder and not a direct complication of DVT.
Acute limb ischemia typically results from arterial occlusion rather than venous thrombosis complications.
Arterial claudication is a symptom of peripheral arterial disease, not a complication of venous thrombosis.
Venous ulceration is a recognized long-term consequence of deep vein thrombosis and post-thrombotic syndrome.
Buerger disease is an inflammatory arterial condition unrelated to deep vein thrombosis complications.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1042: "Subsequently, patients are at risk of developing PTS ( Figure 62.30 ) and venous ulceration."

statement: During the initial stages of venous thrombus formation, what specific component aggregates first to commence the process before fibrin and red cells form a mesh?
optionExplanations: Leukocytes may interact with the endothelium but do not form the initial aggregate of the thrombus.
Fibrinogen is converted to fibrin later in the formation of the thrombus mesh.
Chylomicrons are lipid particles and are not involved in the initiation of venous thrombosis.
Antithrombin is an anticoagulant and does not aggregate to form a thrombus.
The thrombus specifically commences as an aggregate of platelets before other components are involved.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1043: "The thrombus commences as a platelet aggregate. Subse - quently, fbrin and red cells form a mesh until the lumen of the vein wall occludes."

statement: When a coralline thrombus progresses within a vein, it typically forms a loose red fibrin clot. How far is this propagated clot likely to extend within the venous system?
options: Up to the next large venous branch
To the level of the knee
correctOption: Up to the next large venous branch
optionExplanations: The thrombus is likely to extend proximally until it reaches the next large venous branch.
Extension to the common iliac vein is possible but the general rule is to the next major branch.
The extension is determined by venous anatomy rather than just reaching the level of the knee.
Specific measurements like ten centimeters are not used to describe the typical extent of propagation.
The thrombus typically occurs in the deep system and progresses along the path of flow to branches.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1043: "The coralline thrombus then progresses ... as a propagated loose red fbrin clot ... This is likely to extend up to the next large venous branch"

statement: Which anatomical pathway does a detached embolus from a lower leg deep vein thrombosis follow to lodge in the pulmonary arteries?
options: Pulmonary veins, left atrium, right heart
Large veins, vena cava, right heart
Large veins, vena cava, left heart
Portal vein, hepatic vein, vena cava
correctOption: Large veins, vena cava, right heart
optionExplanations: The aorta is part of the arterial system; emboli from leg veins travel through the venous system.
Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood to the left heart; emboli from legs arrive via the vena cava.
Emboli travel through the systemic venous system to the right heart and then into the pulmonary circulation.
The embolus enters the right heart, not the left heart, before reaching the pulmonary arteries.
The portal system is distinct from the systemic venous drainage of the lower limbs.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1043: "In this situation the embolus arising from the lower leg veins becomes detached, passes through the large veins of the limb and vena cava, through the right heart and lodges in the pulmonary arteries."

statement: Following an endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR), a follow-up duplex ultrasonography scan reveals a type II endoleak. Which of the following mechanisms best describes the origin of the blood flow into the aneurysm sac in this specific type of endoleak?
options: Leakage from the proximal attachment site of the stent-graft
Porosity of the graft material allowing serous fluid accumulation
Direct flow from the inferior mesenteric artery retrogradely
A fracture in the main body of the bifurcated stent-graft
Migration of the stent components causing a distal seal failure
correctOption: Direct flow from the inferior mesenteric artery retrogradely
optionExplanations: Leaks from the attachment sites are typically classified as Type I endoleaks.
Graft porosity is associated with type IV endoleaks, not type II.
A type II endoleak involves blood flowing retrogradely into the sac from branches like the inferior mesenteric artery.
Structural failure or fractures of the graft are classified as type III endoleaks.
Migration or retraction of the stent components describes a type Ib endoleak.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1042: "There is a type II endoleak from the inferior mesenteric artery, with blood fowing retrogradely into the aneurysm sac (arrow)."

statement: An elderly patient who underwent EVAR three years ago presents with an enlarging aortic sac. Imaging reveals that the distal limb of the stent-graft has moved. How does the migration of the stent-graft components specifically lead to a type Ib endoleak?
options: It creates a retrograde flow from the internal iliac artery
It leads to a disconnection between the graft components
It triggers an inflammatory response in the aortic wall
It allows blood to enter via the proximal attachment zone
It causes retraction into the sac, breaking the distal seal
correctOption: It causes retraction into the sac, breaking the distal seal
optionExplanations: Retrograde flow from branch vessels characterizes type II endoleaks.
Disconnection between components is classified as a type III endoleak.
Inflammatory responses do not define the mechanical classification of a type Ib endoleak.
Proximal seal failure is a type Ia endoleak, while type Ib involves the distal end.
Migration and retraction of the graft into the aneurysm sac creates a type Ib endoleak and predisposes to rupture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1042: "Figure 61.48 A stent–graft retracted into the aneurysm sac, creating a type Ib endoleak. of the components and migration of the stent–graft, all of which predispose to late rupture"

statement: In the majority of patients who suffer a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm, where does the rupture typically occur anatomically, and what is the primary clinical consequence regarding hospital arrival?
options: Anteriorly into the peritoneal cavity; most patients reach hospital
Superiorly into the thoracic cavity; most reach hospital alive
Anteriorly into the peritoneal cavity; free bleeding allows survival
Posterolaterally into the retroperitoneal space; many die before arrival
Posterolaterally into the retroperitoneal space; survival is likely
correctOption: Posterolaterally into the retroperitoneal space; many die before arrival
optionExplanations: Anterior rupture (20%) results in free bleeding and very few patients reach the hospital alive.
Abdominal aortic aneurysms do not typically rupture superiorly into the thoracic cavity.
Anterior rupture leads to rapid death due to free bleeding into the peritoneal cavity.
80% rupture posterolaterally into the retroperitoneal space, but less than 50% of all rupture patients survive to reach hospital.
While posterolateral rupture is more common, survival to the hospital is still less than 50%.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1042: "Abdominal aortic aneurysms can rupture anteriorly into the peritoneal cavity (20%) or posterolaterally into the retroperitoneal space (80%). Less than 50% of patients with rupture survive to reach hospital."

statement: A clinician is evaluating a patient with severe back pain and a suspected abdominal aortic aneurysm using bedside ultrasonography. The scan clearly visualizes a 7 cm aneurysm. Why is ultrasound considered insufficient as a standalone tool in this acute emergency scenario?
options: It cannot accurately measure the diameter of the aortic sac
It is contraindicated in patients with severe hypotension
It is unable to diagnose the presence of an actual rupture
It cannot differentiate between an aneurysm and a haematoma
It fails to visualize the location of the renal artery origins
correctOption: It is unable to diagnose the presence of an actual rupture
optionExplanations: Ultrasound is generally very good at measuring the diameter of the aortic sac.
Ultrasound is safe and frequently used in hypotensive patients to look for abdominal pathology.
Although ultrasonography can identify the presence of an aneurysm, it cannot confirm whether a rupture has occurred.
It can often see haematomas but cannot confirm the rupture status definitively like CT.
While it may not see renal arteries well, its primary limitation in emergencies is the inability to detect rupture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1042: "If there is doubt about the presence of an aneurysm an ultrasonography scan may help but this cannot diagnose rupture."

statement: A 68-year-old patient has just completed a CT scan which confirms a ruptured infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm. The patient is currently haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate next step in the clinical pathway for this patient?
options: Wait in the radiology suite until cross-matched blood is ready
Insert a urinary catheter in the emergency department bay
Perform a duplex ultrasound to confirm CT scan findings
Transfer immediately to an operating theatre for preparation
Transfer to the intensive care unit for invasive monitoring
correctOption: Transfer immediately to an operating theatre for preparation
optionExplanations: While surgery may be briefly delayed for blood if stable, the patient should still be moved to the theatre first.
Urinary catheters and arterial lines are usually inserted once the patient is in the operating theatre.
CT is the definitive scan; performing further ultrasound would cause unnecessary delay.
The text mandates immediate transfer to the operating theatre after the CT scan for line insertion and prep.
The ICU is not the destination; the patient needs surgical repair immediately.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1043: "After CT scanning, the patient should be transferred immediately to an operating theatre where a urinary catheter and arterial line are usually inserted."

statement: A patient with a ruptured aortic aneurysm presents with significant haemodynamic compromise. The surgical team elects for an endovascular repair. Which adjunct can be utilized during EVAR to gain rapid proximal control in this unstable patient?
options: Insertion of an aortic occlusion balloon catheter
Immediate cross-clamping of the suprarenal aorta
Retrograde infusion of cold saline into the sac
Manual compression of the aorta through the haematoma
correctOption: Insertion of an aortic occlusion balloon catheter
optionExplanations: An aortic occlusion balloon catheter can be used during EVAR to gain control in patients with haemodynamic compromise.
Cross-clamping is a technique used in open surgical repair, not EVAR.
Cold saline infusion is not a standard method for gaining vascular control in AAA rupture.
Vasopressors are supportive but do not provide mechanical control of the bleeding vessel.
Manual compression is an open surgical maneuver, not an endovascular technique.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1043: "Endovascular repair can often be performed under local anaesthetic and, if indicated, an aortic occlusion balloon catheter can be inserted to gain control"

statement: A 66-year-old male presents with persistent back pain and is found to have a 6.0 cm infrarenal aortic aneurysm on CT scan. There is no evidence of rupture or haematoma. How should this patient's surgical timeline be prioritized compared to elective cases?
options: He can be safely managed with blood pressure control alone
Surgery is only indicated if the aneurysm grows by 0.5 cm
Immediate emergency surgery is required within two hours
He should be scheduled for elective repair within two weeks
Surgery should be performed on the next available operating list
correctOption: Surgery should be performed on the next available operating list
optionExplanations: Medical management is insufficient for a symptomatic aneurysm of this size.
Symptoms themselves are an indication for surgery regardless of recent growth rates.
Immediate emergency surgery is reserved for confirmed ruptures; symptomatic ones are urgent but usually scheduled for the next list.
Symptomatic aneurysms require more urgent attention than standard elective cases due to the risk of rupture.
Pain in a symptomatic aneurysm may indicate imminent rupture, necessitating surgery on the next available list.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1043: "Pain may be a warning sign of stretching of the aneurysm sac and imminent rupture; surgery should be performed as soon as possible (usually on the next available operating list)."

statement: While acute kidney injury (AKI) is uncommon after elective abdominal aortic aneurysm repairs, it is a significant risk in other scenarios. Which clinical factor most significantly increases the likelihood of developing AKI following an aortic procedure?
options: The use of endovascular repair instead of open repair
Considerable intraoperative blood loss during the procedure
The presence of a pulsatile abdominal mass on presentation
Development of a type II endoleak from the mesenteric artery
A history of respiratory complications like atelectasis
correctOption: Considerable intraoperative blood loss during the procedure
optionExplanations: AKI is specifically noted as a complication of rupture repairs and blood loss rather than being tied to EVAR specifically.
AKI is more likely if there is preoperative renal impairment or considerable intraoperative blood loss.
A pulsatile mass is a diagnostic sign of rupture, not an independent risk factor for post-op AKI.
Type II endoleaks are a complication of EVAR but are not the primary driver of acute kidney injury.
Respiratory issues are common post-op complications but do not directly cause AKI.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1043: "Acute kidney injury is more likely if there is preoperative renal impairment or considerable intraoperative blood loss."

statement: A patient with an asymptomatic infrarenal aortic aneurysm suddenly develops a painful, blue toe on the right foot, despite having palpable pedal pulses. Which pathological feature of the aneurysm is responsible for this acute presentation?
options: Retrograde flow into the inferior mesenteric artery
Type Ib endoleak from a previously placed stent
Nerve compression by the stretching aneurysm sac
Rupture of the aneurysm into the peritoneal cavity
optionExplanations: Retrograde flow causes endoleaks, not distal limb ischaemia.
Endoleaks cause sac expansion, not typically distal embolic events.
Nerve compression typically causes thigh or groin pain, not ischemic digits.
Rupture presents with hypotension and severe abdominal/back pain, not isolated blue toes.
A few aneurysms cause symptoms through the distal embolisation of intraluminal thrombus.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1043: "Finally, a few cause symptoms from distal embolisation of intraluminal thrombus."

statement: In a patient with a posterolateral rupture of an aortic aneurysm, a brief period of clinical stability is sometimes observed. What physiological mechanism contributes to this temporary arrest of haemorrhage?
options: Spontaneous thrombosis of the entire aneurysm sac
Compression of the inferior vena cava by the mass
A sudden increase in systemic systolic blood pressure
Resistance provided by the retroperitoneal tissues
Reflex vasoconstriction of the mesenteric circulation
correctOption: Resistance provided by the retroperitoneal tissues
optionExplanations: Thrombosis does not arrest the bleed in a rupture; the sac has already failed.
IVC compression would not stop the high-pressure arterial bleed from the aorta.
Higher blood pressure would increase haemorrhage rather than arrest it.
Stability results from a combination of moderate hypotension and the resistance of retroperitoneal tissues against the haematoma.
Vasoconstriction does not provide the mechanical resistance needed to stop an aortic rupture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1042: "Often a brief period ensues when a combination of moderate hypotension and the resistance of the retroperitoneal tissues arrests further haemorrhage"

statement: How is Homans' sign, traditionally associated with the physical assessment for deep vein thrombosis, correctly defined?
options: Tenderness along the course of the femoral vein
Resistance of the calf muscles to forcible dorsiflexion
Cyanosis of the limb upon elevation to forty-five degrees
Inability to maintain ankle dorsiflexion against resistance
Pain in the calf upon passive plantarflexion
correctOption: Resistance of the calf muscles to forcible dorsiflexion
optionExplanations: Tenderness along the deep veins is a separate clinical finding from Homans' sign.
Homans' sign is defined as the resistance of the calf muscles during the maneuver of forcible dorsiflexion.
Skin color changes on elevation relate to arterial insufficiency or other venous conditions, not Homans' sign.
The sign relates to passive resistance to a movement, not the strength of active movement.
The definition focuses on resistance rather than pain and specifically involves dorsiflexion.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1065: "Homans’ sign – resistance (not pain) of the calf muscles to forcible dorsifexion – is not specifc and should not be elicited."

statement: A surgical patient presents with necrosis of the foot. The gangrene is symmetrical, involving all of the toes, and is accompanied by marked edema of the foot without a clear-cut edge. Which diagnosis is most likely?
optionExplanations: Venous gangrene is characterized by symmetry in the toes, marked edema, and the lack of a clear-cut edge.
Diabetic gangrene is often associated with infection or isolated arterial disease rather than this specific edematous symmetrical pattern.
Arterial gangrene usually has a clear-cut line of demarcation and less edema than venous gangrene.
Buerger's disease typically presents with progressive ischemia rather than symmetrical, edematous gangrene.
Raynaud's phenomenon involves reversible vasospasm and rarely results in global symmetrical foot edema with gangrene.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1065: "Figure 62.33 A foot with venous gangrene. The gangrene is symmet - rical, involving all of the toes. There is no clear-cut edge and there is marked oedema of the foot."

statement: A patient with extensive deep vein thrombosis presents with a cyanosed limb and severe swelling. What is the fundamental physiological mechanism indicated by this presentation, known as phlegmasia cerulea dolens?
options: High venous pressures impeding tissue perfusion
Isolated infection of the superficial veins
correctOption: High venous pressures impeding tissue perfusion
optionExplanations: Systemic low protein states cause edema but do not explain the localized cyanosis and impeded perfusion of phlegmasia.
This presentation indicates a worsening, critical state of thrombosis rather than resolution.
This condition indicates that venous pressures have reached levels so high that they physically impede arterial tissue perfusion.
Cellulitis may mimic the appearance, but the physiological impedance is caused by venous pressure, not superficial infection.
Phlegmasia cerulea dolens is a venous complication, though it eventually affects arterial supply due to pressure.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1065: "This indicates venous pressures that are so high they are impeding tissue perfusion. Patients who present with venous gangrene ( Figure 62.33 ) often have an underlying neoplasm."

statement: A patient presents with a chronic venous leg ulcer and superficial reflux. Considering the outcomes of surgical intervention versus standard care, what is the expected clinical benefit of early endovenous ablation?
options: It almost halves the time to healing of the ulcer
It reduces healing time by approximately ten percent
It increases the ulcer recurrence rate by ten percent
It is only indicated for ulcers larger than ten centimeters
It is generally not considered cost-effective
correctOption: It almost halves the time to healing of the ulcer
optionExplanations: Early endovenous ablation of superficial reflux is proven to almost halve the time required for ulcer healing.
The clinical benefit of early ablation is significantly more substantial than a ten percent reduction.
Early ablation actually reduces recurrence rates rather than increasing them.
The indication for ablation is the presence of superficial reflux, regardless of a specific ulcer size threshold.
The procedure is specifically described as being cost-effective in the management of venous ulcers.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1044: "Early endovenous ablation of superfcial refux almost halves the time to healing of venous leg ulcers, reduces ulcer recurrence rates and is cost-effective"

statement: If a patient presents with swelling in both lower limbs, which diagnostic differentiation must be prioritized to distinguish deep vein thrombosis from systemic causes such as renal failure or hypoproteinaemia?
options: The presence of a low-grade pyrexia
The presence of dilated superficial veins
The results of a modified Wells score of zero
The presence of bilateral vs unilateral involvement
correctOption: The presence of bilateral vs unilateral involvement
optionExplanations: Pyrexia can occur in DVT (especially with repeated PE) but is also found in many other conditions.
Dilated superficial veins are a Wells criterion but can also occur in chronic venous hypertension without acute DVT.
A Wells score of zero suggests low probability but does not specifically differentiate DVT from renal failure.
While DVT can be bilateral, its presentation in both legs requires careful differentiation from systemic diseases.
Homans' sign is not specific and should not be used as a primary differentiator for systemic oedema.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1065: "is bilateral, DVT must be diferentiated from other causes of systemic oedema, such as hypoproteinaemia, renal failure and heart failure."

statement: In patients with objectively confirmed deep vein thrombosis, what is the approximate incidence of clinical signs and symptoms specifically associated with pulmonary embolus?
optionExplanations: The textbook identifies that signs and symptoms of pulmonary embolus occur in about 10% of patients with confirmed DVT.
A 1% incidence is an underestimate of the clinical presentation of PE in confirmed DVT cases.
Clinical symptoms of PE are absent in the vast majority (approximately 90%) of patients with confirmed DVT.
50% refers to the incidence of leg pain in DVT patients, not pulmonary embolus symptoms.
Most DVT cases do not present with overt clinical signs of pulmonary embolism.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1065: "Clinical signs and symptoms of pulmonary embolus occur in about 10% of patients with confrmed DVT."

statement: Within the modified Wells criteria used to predict the probability of deep vein thrombosis, which clinical variable is assigned a score of three points, the highest positive weight in the table?
options: Bedridden for more than three days
optionExplanations: Malignancy is a significant risk factor but is only assigned 1 point in the modified Wells criteria.
Immobilization or being bedridden for over 3 days contributes 1 point to the Wells score.
A history of previous DVT is a significant factor but only contributes 1 point to the total score.
Intravenous drug abuse is the only variable in the provided modified Wells criteria table assigned 3 points.
Pitting oedema is a common clinical sign but only accounts for 1 point in the scoring system.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1065: "Intravenous drug abuse 3" (Table 62.4 Modified Wells criteria).

statement: A patient presents with a stiff calf and dilated surface veins. Based on clinical surgical principles, how reliable are these physical signs in confirming a diagnosis of deep vein thrombosis?
options: Highly reliable as they are present in 100% of cases
Diagnostic only when accompanied by a low-grade pyrexia
Unreliable and physical signs may be entirely absent
Completely excluded if the patient has no leg pain
Only reliable if the swelling is strictly limited to the ankle
correctOption: Unreliable and physical signs may be entirely absent
optionExplanations: Physical signs are frequently absent and far from 100% reliable in DVT cases.
Pyrexia is non-specific and does not make unreliable physical signs diagnostic.
Clinical examination for DVT is documented as unreliable, and patients may present with no physical signs at all.
Leg pain is only present in 50% of DVT patients; its absence does not rule out the diagnosis.
Swelling can involve the entire limb or be absent; ankle-only swelling is not a reliability threshold for exam signs.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1065: "Clinical examination for DVT is unreliable. Physical signs may also be absent."

coreConcept: Differential Diagnosis of Deep Vein Thrombosis
statement: A 54-year-old male presents with acute swelling and pain in his right calf. On examination, the clinician notes the presence of a pulsatile mass in the popliteal fossa. Which condition mentioned in the differential diagnosis of venous thrombosis must be excluded to explain this specific clinical finding?
optionExplanations: A thrombosed popliteal aneurysm is specifically listed as a differential diagnosis for DVT in patients with lower limb symptoms.
Arterial ischaemia presents with a cold, pulseless limb rather than a pulsatile mass associated with swelling.
Ruptured Baker cysts typically present with calf pain and swelling but are not associated with a pulsatile popliteal mass.
A ruptured plantaris muscle causes sudden calf pain during activity but does not present as a popliteal aneurysm.
A calf muscle haematoma presents with pain and localized swelling following trauma rather than a pulsatile popliteal mass.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1066: "The diferential diagnosis of a DVT includes a ruptured Baker’s cyst, a calf muscle haematoma, a ruptured plantaris muscle, a thrombosed popliteal aneurysm and arterial isch - aemia."

statement: A 72-year-old patient with a history of severe claudication is admitted for major abdominal surgery. Which prophylactic measure for venous thromboembolism is specifically contraindicated in this patient based on their vascular history?
optionExplanations: LMWH is the standard pharmacological prophylaxis and is not contraindicated by peripheral vascular disease.
Unfractionated heparin is used for pharmacological prophylaxis and is not restricted by peripheral vascular status.
Mobilization is a standard part of recovery and is not contraindicated by the presence of peripheral vascular disease.
Compression-based measures like pneumatic compression or stockings must be avoided in patients with peripheral vascular disease.
Oral NOACs are used for treatment or prophylaxis and are not contraindicated by peripheral vascular disease.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1066: "Compression-based prophylactic measures should be avoided in patients with peripheral vascular disease."

coreConcept: VTE Risk Stratification: High Risk Group
statement: Based on the risk stratification for venous thromboembolism, which clinical scenario places a patient specifically into the high-risk group requiring pharmacological prophylaxis?
options: Major surgery in a 35-year-old with no risk factors
Minor surgery in a 30-year-old with no risk factors
Major surgery in a 45-year-old with no risk factors
Major surgery for inflammatory bowel disease
optionExplanations: Major surgery in patients under age 40 with no other risk factors is classified as low risk.
Minor surgery in a patient of any age without risk factors is classified as a low-risk scenario.
Major surgery in a patient age 40+ with no other risk factors is classified as a medium-risk scenario.
Major abdominal or pelvic surgery for cancer is explicitly listed as a high-risk category in Table 62.6.
Major medical illnesses like inflammatory bowel disease are categorized under the medium-risk group.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1067: "High... Major abdominal/pelvic surgery for cancer"

statement: Although rarely required in modern practice, what is the characteristic radiological appearance of a thrombus during ascending venography?
options: Increased contrast uptake in the vessel wall
Extravasation of contrast into the calf muscle
Complete absence of the vein on imaging
A filling defect with contrast passing around it
Dilation of the vein proximal to the thrombus
correctOption: A filling defect with contrast passing around it
optionExplanations: Venography visualizes the lumen via contrast; wall uptake is not the primary diagnostic feature for thrombus.
Extravasation indicates vessel rupture, not the presence of an intraluminal thrombus.
While a thrombus blocks flow, the specific visual sign described is a filling defect, not total absence.
The text and Figure 62.34 describe a thrombus as a filling defect with contrast passing around it.
Venous dilation may occur, but the classic description for the thrombus itself is a filling defect.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1066: "Ascending venography, which shows a thrombus as a fll - ing defect... Figure 62.34 ... showing flling defects (arrows) with contrast passing around the thrombus."

statement: Under the modified Wells criteria for predicting pulmonary embolism, what is the score assigned for a patient who has received treatment for malignancy within the past 6 months?
optionExplanations: A score of 2 is not listed for any individual component in the provided Wells criteria table.
There is no 0.5 score assigned for any variable in the modified Wells table.
Three points are assigned for clinical signs of DVT or if an alternative diagnosis is less likely.
Malignancy (treatment or palliation within the past 6 months) is assigned a score of 1.
A score of 1.5 is assigned for heart rate, immobilization, or previous DVT/PE history.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1066: "Malignancy (treatment or palliation within past 6 months) [Score] 1"

statement: A patient presents with a sudden onset of symptoms in the right lower extremity. Which specific combination of clinical findings characteristically identifies an acutely ischaemic foot as opposed to a chronically ischaemic one?
options: Swollen, purple, and associated with rest pain
Equilibrated temperature, red, and intact sensation
optionExplanations: These features suggest chronic dependency or venous congestion rather than acute arterial occlusion.
Acute limb ischemia is classically characterized by being cold, white, paralysed, and insensate due to the sudden loss of perfusion.
Mummified black tissue describes dry gangrene, a late stage of chronic limb-threatening ischemia.
These features are contrary to the presentation of acute ischemia.
Chronically ischaemic limbs tend to equilibrate with surroundings and maintain sensation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1020: "Unlike an acutely ischaemic foot that is often cold, white, paralysed and insensate, a chronically ischaemic limb tends to equilibrate with the temperature of its surroundings and may feel quite warm under the bedclothes."

statement: During a vascular examination, a clinician suspects severe ischemia and performs a limb elevation test. Which specific morphological change in the dorsal foot veins occurs upon elevation to confirm a severe reduction in perfusion pressure?
optionExplanations: Rapid refill is a sign of good perfusion, the opposite of what is seen in severe ischemia.
Fixed mottling indicates non-viable tissue, but it is not the specific venous sign elicited by elevation.
Venous return is not pulsatile; this finding does not relate to the assessment of severe ischemia via elevation.
Engorgement suggests venous insufficiency or dependency, not severe arterial ischemia upon elevation.
Venous guttering occurs when arterial perfusion is insufficient to maintain venous filling against gravity during elevation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1020: "However, elevation of the limb reveals the severity of the ischaemia with venous guttering and foot pallor that changes to a red/ purple colour when the limb is allowed to hang down again (dependent rubor or the sunset foot)"

statement: Following the elevation of a severely ischaemic limb, the foot is allowed to hang down in a dependent position. What specific color change defines the sunset foot phenomenon in this clinical sequence?
options: Changes to a red or purple colour
Immediately returns to a healthy pink
correctOption: Changes to a red or purple colour
optionExplanations: Persistent pallor suggests ongoing severe ischemia but is not the definition of the sunset foot itself.
Dependent rubor or sunset foot is the red/purple discoloration that occurs as blood returns to a maximally dilated capillary bed.
A healthy pink return would indicate normal perfusion rather than the severity of ischemia being tested.
Yellowing is not a sign of arterial ischemia or dependent rubor.
Petechiae are not the characteristic color change described for the sunset foot.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1020: "However, elevation of the limb reveals the severity of the ischaemia with venous guttering and foot pallor that changes to a red/ purple colour when the limb is allowed to hang down again (dependent rubor or the sunset foot)"

statement: When arterial perfusion is so severely compromised that symptoms occur even at rest, what metabolic process is primarily responsible for the production of pain in the affected muscle groups?
optionExplanations: Aerobic processes cannot be maintained in the state of severe ischemia leading to rest pain.
Anaerobic respiration occurs when oxygen delivery is insufficient, leading to the accumulation of metabolites that cause pain.
While catabolism occurs in starvation, it is not the primary mechanism of acute ischaemic pain.
Gluconeogenesis is a metabolic pathway for glucose production, not the cause of ischaemic pain.
Oxidative phosphorylation is the normal aerobic pathway that fails during severe ischemia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1020: "As disease progression occurs the claudication distance decreases and perfusion to the leg may be so severely compromised that anaerobic respiration occurs even at rest, typically afecting the foot and/or calf."

statement: A patient presents with sudden lower limb pain. The clinician determines the severity of symptoms is likely high because the occlusion occurred in a previously normal artery without time for compensation. What developmental feature is missing in this acute event compared to chronic stenosis?
optionExplanations: Atherosclerotic plaque is the cause of chronic stenosis, but its absence explains why the artery was previously normal.
Capillary structures do not provide the bypass flow needed to abate symptoms of arterial occlusion.
Intimal thickening is a chronic change, not a compensatory mechanism that abates symptoms like collaterals do.
Venous valves are unrelated to the compensation of arterial occlusion.
Acute ischemia is severe because there is no time for the development of alternative collateral routes that provide blood flow.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 998: "In chronic stenosis symptoms may be abated despite being afected by signifcant steno-occlusive disease as a result of the development of a collateral circulation that provides an alternative, albeit less efective, route for blood to reach the target tissue/organ"

statement: An elderly patient with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI) presents with a red, swollen foot after sitting for several hours. A junior clinician incorrectly diagnoses cellulitis. Which simple clinical maneuver would most effectively differentiate this as dependent rubor?
options: Testing for sensation in the toes
Checking for a dorsalis pedis pulse
Measuring the temperature with a probe
Applying pressure to check for pitting edema
optionExplanations: Sensation is usually intact in chronic ischemia (CLTI), so it does not differentiate rubor from cellulitis.
Pulses may be absent in both chronic ischemia and obscured by swelling in cellulitis; elevation is more specific for rubor.
While temperature varies, elevation is the definitive physical maneuver to unmask ischemia hidden by dependent rubor.
Elevation causes the rubor to disappear and reveals the underlying pallor and venous guttering in severe ischemia.
Pitting edema may be present in both conditions and does not distinguish the underlying vascular cause.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1020: "Patients with CLTI who have been waiting for a consultation with their leg in dependence may have a red swollen foot that may be mistaken for cellulitis by the unwary clinician. However, elevation of the limb reveals the severity of the ischaemia with venous guttering"

statement: A patient with severe arterial disease finds that even the weight of bedclothes on their foot becomes intolerable at night. This hyperesthesia is most likely an exacerbation of which underlying condition?
optionExplanations: Osteoarthritis pain is mechanical and related to joint movement, not the weight of fabric.
Leriche’s syndrome refers specifically to aortoiliac disease symptoms like buttock claudication and impotence.
Intermittent claudication is pain brought on by walking and relieved by rest.
Venous hypertension typically causes heaviness and swelling, not the acute intolerance of touch seen in ischaemic rest pain.
Rest pain is so severe that external pressure from bedclothes can exacerbate the baseline discomfort caused by ischemia.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1020: "The patient characteristically describes pain that is worse at night... Even the pressure of bedclothes on the foot may exacerbate the pain."

statement: When examining a patient with severe, untreated limb ischemia, a clinician observes blackened, mummified tissues on the toes. What factor would most likely transition this presentation from dry to wet gangrene?
optionExplanations: Dry dressings are intended to maintain dryness; they would not promote wet gangrene.
Restoration of flow might save remaining tissue but does not automatically turn dry gangrene wet.
Elevation would decrease perfusion further but is not the specific trigger for the wet type of gangrene.
Infection in the necrotic tissue introduces moisture and inflammatory products, making the gangrene wet.
Increased collateral flow would improve the state of the limb, not worsen the gangrene type.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1020: "The blackened mummifed tissues of frank gangrene are unmistakable ( Figure 61.4 ), and superadded infection often makes the gangrene wet."

statement: In the assessment of a patient with a newly occluded artery, which pair of factors is most critical in determining whether the patient presents with mild claudication or immediate, limb-threatening acute ischemia?
options: Duration of rest and atmospheric temperature
Presence of venous valves and heart rate
Patient age and blood glucose level
Size of the vessel and speed of occlusion
Type of footwear and distance walked
correctOption: Size of the vessel and speed of occlusion
optionExplanations: These factors may influence comfort but do not determine the severity of the arterial blockage itself.
Venous valves are irrelevant to the arterial supply, and heart rate is a secondary factor.
While important for health, these are not the primary determinants of the immediate severity of an arterial occlusion.
The severity of symptoms relates directly to the size of the artery blocked and how quickly the occlusion occurs (acute vs chronic).
These relate to the clinical assessment of claudication but not the fundamental severity of the vascular event.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 998: "The severity of the symptoms relates to the size of the vessel occluded and whether the stenosis or occlusion occurs suddenly (acute) in a previously normal artery or gradually (chronic)"

statement: A clinician is differentiating between types of leg ulcers. Which location and appearance are most characteristic of ulcers caused by severe arterial insufficiency?
options: Shallow ulcers on the dorsum of the feet and around the malleoli
Multiple small ulcers on the proximal thigh
Deep ulcers with heavy granulation on the posterior calf
Highly exudative ulcers in the gaiter area with hyperpigmentation
Painless ulcers located exclusively on the plantar surface
correctOption: Shallow ulcers on the dorsum of the feet and around the malleoli
optionExplanations: Ischaemic ulcers typically present on the dorsum of the feet, between toes, or around the malleoli.
Ischemia usually affects the distal aspects of the limb first; thigh ulcers are not characteristic.
Arterial ulcers are usually painful and lack robust granulation due to poor blood supply.
Gaiter area ulcers with hyperpigmentation are classic for venous, not arterial, insufficiency.
Arterial ulcers are notoriously painful; painless plantar ulcers are more suggestive of neuropathy.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1020: "Ulceration occurs with severe arterial insufciency and may present as painful erosions between the toes or as shallow, non-healing ulcers on the dorsum of the feet, on the shins and especially around the malleoli."

statement: A patient is evaluated for limb pain. The clinician finds that the limb temperature is the same as the room but sensation is completely intact and there is no paralysis. This finding helps rule out which condition?
optionExplanations: Aortoiliac disease is a chronic condition and would not typically present with the acute features of paralysis.
Intermittent claudication does not involve loss of sensation or paralysis.
Leriche’s syndrome is a chronic condition characterized by claudication and impotence, not acute sensory loss.
Acute limb ischemia typically causes a loss of sensation and paralysis, whereas chronic forms usually leave sensation intact.
Chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI) often presents with intact sensation and no paralysis.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1020: "Chronic ischaemia does not produce paralysis and sensation is usually intact. ... Unlike an acutely ischaemic foot that is often... paralysed and insensate"

statement: Which artery is most commonly affected by atherosclerosis and/or thromboembolic disease leading to lower limb ischemia in 70% of cases?
optionExplanations: Aortoiliac disease (including the common iliac) occurs in about 30% of cases.
Internal iliac disease relates to pelvic symptoms and Leriche syndrome but is not the most common lower limb site.
Aortic disease is less common than distal femoral disease in peripheral arterial presentations.
The profunda femoris is often a source of collaterals rather than the primary site of occlusion in the majority of cases.
The superficial femoral artery is the most frequent site of disease, accounting for approximately 70% of cases.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 998: "The muscle group afected by claudication is classically one anatomical level below the level of arterial disease and is usually felt in the posterior calf as the superfcial femoral artery is the most commonly afected artery (70% of cases)."

coreConcept: Differentiating Ischaemic Pain from Nerve Compression
statement: A 70-year-old man experiences leg pain when walking. The clinician notes that the pain is relieved only when the patient sits down and takes longer than 5 minutes to subside. This pattern is most suggestive of which condition rather than arterial claudication?
optionExplanations: Spinal stenosis or nerve compression is typically relieved only by sitting and usually takes longer than 5 minutes to resolve.
Leriche's syndrome presents with buttock claudication which follows the standard arterial recovery pattern.
Arterial claudication is typically relieved within 5 minutes and can be relieved by simply standing still.
Anemia reduces oxygen delivery but does not change the classic recovery pattern of mechanical nerve compression.
Acute limb ischemia causes constant pain that is not intermittent or relieved by rest.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 998: "relieved by rest in both the standing and sitting positions, usually within 5 minutes (unlike nerve compression from a lumbar intervertebral disc prolapse or osteoarthritis of the spine or spinal stenosis, which are typically relieved only when resting in the sitting position for longer than 5 minutes)."

statement: A male patient presents with buttock claudication. What additional clinical finding would complete the classic description of Leriche’s syndrome?
optionExplanations: Wet gangrene is a complication of severe ischemia/infection, not a specific component of Leriche's syndrome.
Venous guttering is a sign of severe distal ischemia, not a core definition of this syndrome.
Elevational pallor is a general sign of severe ischemia, not unique to Leriche's syndrome.
Leriche’s syndrome is the specific combination of buttock claudication and sexual impotence due to aortoiliac disease.
Paralysis is an acute finding, whereas Leriche's is a chronic disease presentation.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 998: "Aortoiliac disease (30% of cases) may cause thigh or buttock claudication; Leriche’s syndrome is buttock claudication com - bined with sexual impotence, which is secondary to arterial insufciency"

coreConcept: Acute Limb Ischemia: Surgical Access for Open Repair
statement: A patient with acute limb ischemia secondary to an infrarenal aneurysm is scheduled for open repair. To achieve optimal exposure of the aorta and common iliac arteries under general anesthesia, which surgical incision and initial abdominal maneuver are most appropriate?
options: Left flank incision; rotate the liver medially
Full-length midline incision; lift the small bowel to the right
Infraumbilical transverse incision; lift the stomach superiorly
McBurney incision; mobilize the cecum posteriorly
Right paramedian incision; lift the large bowel to the left
correctOption: Full-length midline incision; lift the small bowel to the right
optionExplanations: Standard open repair is performed supine via midline or transverse incision, not a flank approach.
A full-length midline or supraumbilical transverse incision allows the small bowel to be shifted right to identify the aorta.
The incision should be supraumbilical if transverse, and the small bowel is the primary structure moved.
A McBurney incision is for appendectomy and provides no access to the aorta.
The standard approach is midline or supraumbilical transverse, and the small bowel is moved right.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1040: "Open aneurysm repair Under general anaesthesia, with the patient lying supine, a full-length midline or supraumbilical transverse incision is made. The small bowel is lifted to the patient’s right and the aorta identifed."

coreConcept: Acute Limb Ischemia: Anticoagulation during Definitive Surgery
statement: During the open surgical management of an infrarenal aneurysm to treat acute limb ischemia, when should systemic heparin ideally be administered relative to the application of vascular clamps?
options: Only if distal pulses do not return after clamp release
Immediately after the aneurysm sac is opened
After the aortic prosthesis is sutured
At the time of induction of general anesthesia
optionExplanations: Systemic heparin (3000–5000 U) is typically given before clamping to protect the distal bed.
Waiting until after clamp release is too late to prevent intraoperative thrombosis.
Heparin must be circulating before clamping to prevent stasis-induced thrombosis.
Heparinization is required during the clamping period, not after the graft is finished.
Anesthesia induction is too early; it is given specifically before the vascular occlusion phase.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1040: "Many surgeons give systemic heparin (3000–5000 U) before clamping."

coreConcept: Acute Limb Ischemia: Graft Selection for Extensive Disease
statement: A patient undergoing open repair for an abdominal aneurysm causing limb ischemia is found to have severe atheroma and dilatation extending into both common iliac arteries. If a simple aortoaortic tube graft is insufficient, what is the next appropriate modification for reconstruction?
options: Ligation of the common iliac arteries and axillobifemoral bypass
Replacement of the aorta with a venous autograft
Primary anastomosis of the aorta to the internal iliac arteries
Endovascular stenting of the iliac arteries only
Construction of an aortobi-iliac or aortobifemoral bypass
correctOption: Construction of an aortobi-iliac or aortobifemoral bypass
optionExplanations: Axillobifemoral is usually reserved for infected fields or patients unfit for major abdominal surgery.
Aortic reconstruction uses synthetic prostheses (Dacron/PTFE), not venous autografts.
The reconstruction must bypass the diseased iliac segments to the distal iliacs or femorals.
In open repair, the goal is definitive surgical reconstruction, not just focal stenting.
If the iliac vessels are involved with dilatation or severe atheroma, an aortobi-iliac or aortobifemoral bypass is constructed.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1040: "Occasionally, when the iliac vessels are also involved with dilatation or severe atheroma, it is necessary to construct an aortobi-iliac or aortobifemoral bypass, rather than use a simple aortoaortic tube."

coreConcept: Acute Limb Ischemia: Prevention of Post-Surgical Fistula
statement: Following successful graft interposition during open repair of an aneurysm, the surgeon evaluates the risk of future adherence between the prosthetic material and the bowel. Which step is most effective to reduce the risk of potential fistula formation?
options: Leaving the aneurysm sac open to drain into the peritoneum
Closing the aneurysm sac around the prosthesis
Omental wrapping of the proximal anastomosis only
Placing a layer of oxidized cellulose over the graft
Irrigating the abdomen with antibiotic solution
correctOption: Closing the aneurysm sac around the prosthesis
optionExplanations: Leaving the sac open increases the risk of the bowel coming into direct contact with the synthetic graft.
Closing the aneurysm sac excludes the prosthesis and suture lines from the bowel, reducing adherence and fistula risk.
Omental wrapping is an option but the primary method described is using the native sac.
Cellulose does not provide the same structural barrier as the native aneurysm sac.
Irrigation helps prevent infection but does not address the mechanical adherence of the graft to the bowel.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1040: "If haemostasis is satisfactory at this point, the aneurysm sac is closed around the prosthesis to exclude both it and the suture lines from the bowel to reduce the risk of adherence and potential fstula formation."

coreConcept: Acute Limb Ischemia: Aortic Exposure Landmarks
statement: While exposing the upper limit of an infrarenal aneurysm for clamp placement, the surgeon identifies a large venous structure crossing the aorta. Which anatomical landmark generally defines the upper limit of exposure for an infrarenal repair?
options: The left renal vein and renal arteries
correctOption: The left renal vein and renal arteries
optionExplanations: The IMV is not the primary landmark used to identify the proximal neck for infrarenal clamping.
The SMA is superior to the infrarenal neck and is usually avoided in standard infrarenal repairs.
The celiac axis is much higher than the infrarenal neck.
Hepatic veins are near the diaphragm and not relevant to infrarenal aortic exposure.
The aorta immediately above the dilatation is generally exposed just inferior to the left renal vein and renal arteries.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1040: "The aorta immediately above the dilatation is exposed; this is generally just inferior to the left renal vein and renal arteries ( Figure 61.43 )."

statement: A patient undergoes endovascular repair (EVAR) of an aneurysm that previously caused micro-embolization and limb ischemia. Which post-operative requirement is most critical to prevent late rupture and detect graft-related complications?
options: A second-stage open repair after 6 years
Daily aspirin and clopidogrel for the duration of the patient's life
Routine replacement of the endovascular prosthesis every 10 years
Lifelong follow-up and surveillance with duplex or CT scans
correctOption: Lifelong follow-up and surveillance with duplex or CT scans
optionExplanations: EVAR is the definitive treatment; open repair is only indicated if EVAR fails or ruptures.
Antiplatelets are common but do not replace the need for imaging surveillance to detect structural graft failure.
Prostheses are meant to be permanent, though they require monitoring.
Patients require lifelong surveillance with duplex or CT to detect endoleaks, migration, or disconnection which predispose to late rupture.
Invasive angiography is not the standard for routine lifelong surveillance.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1040: "Patients who undergo EVAR require lifelong follow-up and surveillance with duplex ( Figure 61.47 ) or CT scans to detect endoleak, disconnection of the components and migration of the stent–graft, all of which predispose to late rupture"

coreConcept: Acute Limb Ischemia: Limitations of Angiography
statement: A patient with limb ischemia undergoes digital subtraction angiography (DSA) which shows a near-normal aortic diameter. However, subsequent CT shows a large aneurysm. What is the most likely pathological reason for this discrepancy?
options: The use of non-ionic contrast medium
Dilation of the adventitia without luminal change
High-velocity jet flow through the aneurysm neck
Systemic hypotension during the angiogram procedure
Presence of a large mural thrombus within the aneurysm
correctOption: Presence of a large mural thrombus within the aneurysm
optionExplanations: Contrast type does not affect the visualization of the anatomical lumen versus the mural thrombus.
The lumen usually appears normal on angiography if thrombus is present, even if the total diameter is increased.
Jet flow might affect image quality but does not explain why the diameter appears smaller.
Hypotension would not selectively mask aneurysm diameter on an angiogram.
Thrombus within the aneurysm can give a false impression of a normal diameter on digital subtraction angiography because only the patent lumen is visualized.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1040: "...this thrombus is the reason an angiogram may give a false impression of aneurysm diameter on digital subtraction angiography (b) ."

coreConcept: Acute Limb Ischemia: Suture Material for Aortic Repair
statement: In the open surgical repair of an infrarenal aneurysm, which type of suture is standard for performing the end-to-end anastomosis between the aortic neck and the prosthesis?
optionExplanations: Catgut is absorbable and unsuitable for vascular anastomoses.
Braided silk is non-absorbable but can harbor infection and has less durability than monofilament synthetic for large vessels.
An aortic prosthesis is sutured end-to-end inside the sac with a monofilament non-absorbable suture.
Absorbable materials are contraindicated for major vascular reconstructions.
Absorbable sutures would fail over time in a high-pressure arterial environment.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1040: "Upper and lower aortic necks are prepared to which an aortic prosthesis is then sutured end-to-end inside the sac with a monoflament non-absorbable suture ( Figure 61.44 )."

coreConcept: Acute Limb Ischemia: Anatomy of Clamping
statement: To exclude an infrarenal aneurysm from the circulation during open surgery, the surgeon must place vascular clamps. Based on the anatomical description of a standard repair, where are these clamps distal to the lesion most commonly applied?
options: The femoral arteries in the groin
optionExplanations: Femoral clamping is used for aortobifemoral bypass, not standard infrarenal repair.
The common iliac arteries are exposed and clamps applied above and below the lesion (aorta above, iliacs below).
The popliteal arteries are far distal and not relevant for aneurysm exclusion.
External iliacs are distal to the common iliacs and are not the first choice for clamping in standard repair.
Internal iliacs are generally not the primary site for distal clamps in standard repair.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1040: "The common iliac arteries are then exposed and clamps applied above and below the lesion."

coreConcept: Acute Limb Ischemia: EVAR Deployment Technique
statement: During the deployment of an endovascular stent-graft, a surgeon inflates a moulding balloon catheter within the prosthesis. What is the primary purpose of this specific technical modification?
options: To thrombose the aneurysm sac immediately
To ensure that hooks and barbs are engaged for a good seal
To measure the internal diameter of the aorta
To dilate the femoral arteries for graft removal
To deliver local heparin to the renal arteries
correctOption: To ensure that hooks and barbs are engaged for a good seal
optionExplanations: The balloon is for graft fixation, not for inducing sac thrombosis.
Some surgeons inflate a moulding balloon to ensure hooks/barbs are engaged and a good seal is obtained against the aortic wall.
Measurements are done via CT and angiogram before and during deployment, not with a moulding balloon.
Moulding balloons are used inside the graft, not for femoral artery dilation.
Balloons are for mechanical fixation, not drug delivery.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 1040: "...some surgeons infate a moulding balloon catheter in the stent–graft to ensure that the hooks and barbs are engaged and a good seal is obtained ( Figure 61.46 )."
